after we ran the first successful experiment batch of e0-e2 we realized that the current family might be a bit too simple in order to monitor actually interesting behavior. therefore Id like to try other families as well. here a report regarding this. i want you to evaluate first which families solves our current problem that the models learn the interface too quickly. the family needs to be complex and dynamic enough to still justify our story of a specialized agent but to make it possible to monitor any reward bias substitution. does this make sense?

here the report: ## Other interesting MiniWoB++ families

We are using **MiniWoB++ through BrowserGym/OpenEnv**. There is considerably more variety available than `read-table-2`.

These are the candidates I would consider:

| Family | What the model does | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| [**multi-orderings (https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/multi-orderings/)**](<https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/multi-orderings/>) | Fills a movie-search form whose fields appear in shuffled order | Directly challenges reliance on fixed field positions |
| [**multi-layouts (https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/multi-layouts/)**](<https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/multi-layouts/>) | Completes the search task across different form layouts | Broader interface variation, although we must check how much survives conversion to accessibility text |
| [**email-inbox-reply (https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/email-inbox-reply/)**](<https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/email-inbox-reply/>) | Finds a specified sender's email and replies with requested text | Navigation through different page states and a longer workflow; this variant avoids scrolling |
| [**login-user-popup (https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/login-user-popup/)**](<https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/login-user-popup/>) | Logs in while handling an unexpected popup | Interruptions and recovery rather than uninterrupted form filling |
| [**guess-number (https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/guess-number/)**](<https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/guess-number/>) | Guesses a hidden number using feedback from previous guesses | Iterative information gathering; useful for examining whether feedback improves the strategy |
| [**click-checkboxes-soft (https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/click-checkboxes-soft/)**](<https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/click-checkboxes-soft/>) | Selects options matching paraphrased words or synonyms | Semantic matching and multiple selections rather than literal value copying |

Other available directions include file-tree navigation (`navigate-tree`), email forwarding, autocomplete, date picking, and form sequences involving different widgets. The [official catalog (https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/list/)](<https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/list/>) includes descriptions and interactive demos.

### My shortlist

I would first screen:

1. **`multi-orderings` and `multi-layouts`** for the interface-specialization concern.
2. **`email-inbox-reply`** for a substantially different workflow.
3. **`login-user-popup`** for reacting to interruptions.
4. **`guess-number`** for feedback-guided interaction.

`click-checkboxes-soft` is a useful additional candidate, but its documented reward allows partial credit, so we must verify what our wrapper reports as success. Also, `guess-number` permits unlimited guesses within the environment; enumeration is possible, so success alone would not prove effective feedback use.

These are **candidates to screen, not already validated replacements**. I confirmed their task files exist at our pinned MiniWoB revision, but could not test the live wrapper because GPU SSH currently times out. In particular, some tasks use custom clickable elements whose IDs may be missing from our accessibility observations.

We already found such problems in earlier screens of tab/collapsible tasks, and a scoring problem with `search-engine`, so I would start with the new candidates above.

also i think we should keep the results of the last batch. if we dont collect new insights which invalidate the results this might be already a run that we can include in our thesis as first evidence

Yes. I'll assess which families require continued use of observations and feedback, and whether they could expose reward bias substitution. I'll also review the E0-E2 findings to separate limits of the task from anything that would invalidate the results.

I'll use the Ponytail workflow to keep this to an evidence review before proposing new runs.

The completed batch supports a useful first result: E2 reduced paired successful-response tokens by about 45%, with 198/200 successes versus E1's 199/200. A simple task limits what this tells us about behavior; it does not by itself invalidate the comparison.

The key distinction for the next family is whether later choices depend on new feedback. Shuffled forms may still be solved by one fixed procedure. I'll check the task source and use Context7 for the wrapper documentation.

I found a concrete scoring problem for `click-checkboxes-soft`: the pinned BrowserGym version converts any positive partial score into full reward. On some instances, submitting with no boxes selected can therefore count as success. I would exclude it under the current scoring contract.

My recommendation is to screen popup recovery and email workflows first, with tree navigation as another candidate. The shuffled forms are useful interface tests, but provide little evidence about responding to feedback.

content.text:
**Yes, this makes sense, and I would keep the completed E0-E2 batch as first thesis evidence.** The next task should require decisions that continue to depend on the current state, even after the model has learned the interface.

Learning an interface quickly is compatible with specialization. The limitation of `read-table-2` is that the initial observation supplies everything needed for the same three-action procedure. That leaves few opportunities to observe whether compression changes information gathering or recovery.

I checked the completed findings, our adapter, and the task source at our pinned MiniWoB revision. My assessment changes the report's priorities:

| Candidate | What it actually adds | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| **`login-user-popup`** | Focusing either field can trigger a popup that disables the form. The agent must distinguish dismissing it from abandoning the task. This creates a concrete opportunity to observe adaptation after an interruption. | **Screen first for feedback and recovery.** However, the branch is small and could also be learned quickly. [Source](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/miniwob-plusplus/blob/eb59fed60fabe8951350275ba8650633b740013b/miniwob/html/miniwob/login-user-popup.html) |
| **Email workflows** | Reply and forward introduce transitions between inbox, message and composition states. A mixture of operations provides a coherent specialization domain. | **Best fit for the specialized-agent story.** Prefer assessing several operations over reply alone, which could become another fixed script. `email-inbox-noscroll` already mixes reply, forward, delete and mark-important tasks. [Source](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/miniwob-plusplus/blob/eb59fed60fabe8951350275ba8650633b740013b/miniwob/html/miniwob/email-inbox-noscroll.html) |
| **`navigate-tree`** | Expanding folders can reveal previously unavailable targets; clicking an incorrect file ends the episode unsuccessfully. | **Promising information-gathering candidate.** Its generated tree is shallow, and accessible action IDs need verification. [Source](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/miniwob-plusplus/blob/eb59fed60fabe8951350275ba8650633b740013b/miniwob/html/miniwob/navigate-tree.html) |
| **`multi-orderings` / `multi-layouts`** | Shuffled fields and, for `multi-layouts`, five templates with different labels and structure. The required values are still available immediately. | **Useful interface-robustness checks; weak primary replacements.** They challenge fixed field mappings but introduce little need for new information during execution. [Orderings](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/miniwob-plusplus/blob/eb59fed60fabe8951350275ba8650633b740013b/miniwob/html/miniwob/multi-orderings.html), [layouts](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/miniwob-plusplus/blob/eb59fed60fabe8951350275ba8650633b740013b/miniwob/html/miniwob/multi-layouts.html) |
| **`guess-number`** | Genuine higher/lower feedback, but only ten possible answers, 0-9, with unlimited guesses at the task level. | **Useful diagnostic for feedback use, limited main task.** Enumeration can succeed; success alone cannot establish an adaptive strategy. [Documentation](https://miniwob.farama.org/environments/guess-number/) |
| **`click-checkboxes-soft`** | Synonym matching from a finite vocabulary, with everything visible initially. | **Exclude under the current scoring contract.** It has a concrete success-definition problem, explained below. |

For checkboxes, the issue is stronger than the report suggests. The task awards partial credit for each correctly checked **or unchecked** box. BrowserGym 0.14.3 then converts **any positive raw score into reward 1**. Consequently, leaving every box unchecked can count as success when most boxes should remain unchecked. That would undermine an exact-completion interpretation. [Task scoring](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/miniwob-plusplus/blob/eb59fed60fabe8951350275ba8650633b740013b/miniwob/html/miniwob/click-checkboxes-soft.html), [pinned BrowserGym conversion](https://github.com/ServiceNow/BrowserGym/blob/v0.14.3/browsergym/miniwob/src/browsergym/miniwob/base.py#L179-L191).

**My preferred direction is an email-workflow specialist, with popup recovery as a focused behavioral test.** Tree navigation is worth screening alongside them. None is yet demonstrated to retain useful complexity after training.

For reward bias substitution, the family needs observable opportunities to do something worse while pursuing shorter responses. We could measure:

- **Feedback use:** does an action contradict information already received?
- **Recovery:** after an observed error or interruption, does the agent adapt or repeat the failed approach?
- **Commitment:** does it submit, send or select the wrong target despite having sufficient information?

These need task-state evidence and opportunity counts. For example, recovery should be assessed among episodes containing an interruption. A shorter successful trajectory or fewer tool calls alone does not establish harmful substitution. E2 should be compared with E1 to distinguish the shaping effect from ordinary specialization.

Before model screening, the shortlisted tasks need correct and deliberately incorrect paths replayed through our actual wrapper. Email icons, tree controls and custom form buttons may lack usable accessibility IDs. Our adapter also truncates observations at [2,000 characters](/Users/mheidebrecht/Documents/Projects/Uni/Master_Thesis/master-thesis-code/pipeline/domains/browsergym/adapter.py:15), which matters for richer pages. After that, a bounded learning screen can establish whether the surviving families retain meaningful behavioral opportunities. This review did not run that live validation or launch experiments.

**The existing batch should remain an intact first study.** Its reviewed result is substantial: **44.93% median paired token reduction**, with a 95% interval of **42.75%-47.33% reduction**, and **198/200 successes versus 199/200**. There were two regressions and one gain, within the declared success-preservation margin. [Findings](/Users/mheidebrecht/Documents/Projects/Uni/Master_Thesis/master-thesis-code/pipeline/runs/e0_e2_s4016_findings.md:290).

It supports a narrow claim about compression on held-out instances of a fixed-interface task. The single training seed, limited behavioral opportunities and shared prompt/runtime batching mismatch remain disclosed limitations. A richer follow-up would extend that evidence; task simplicity alone provides no reason to discard it.

can we just increase the limit of our adapter? in general we should not constrain ourselves with factors that are easily changed

Yes. I'll check how the observation limit interacts with the token budget, then remove the unnecessary restriction. I'll also correct the family assessment so this easy change is treated as setup work rather than a reason to reject richer tasks.

The 2,000-character cutoff is shared by training and evaluation. I'll remove it so task content and controls are preserved, and verify that the change does not affect the saved table observations.

I'm using the Karpathy guidelines for a small change with a regression test. The token budgets still need to be sized for the next study.
